https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.text: View image in fullscreen Kyiv, Ukraine People hold flares during a memorial event at Independence Square in Kyiv, marking the fourth anniversary of the Olenivka prison attack . On 29 July 2022, dozens of Ukrainian soldiers died in the bombardment of the Russian-controlled jail of Olenivka in the eastern Donetsk region. Photograph: Genya Savilov/AFP/Getty Images Share View image in fullscreen Lviv, Ukraine A woman is in tears upon seeing an apartment building hit by a Russian missile strike in Lviv. Donald ⁠Trump cast doubt this week on allowing Ukraine to build Patriot missiles , saying in an interview he was ‘not sure’ about the move. The US president told the Financial Times: ‘It’s a ​very extraordinary weapon, and we have to be ⁠a little bit careful ​of who ​we licence ​to.’ Photograph: Roman Baluk/Reuters Share View image in fullscreen Odesa, Ukraine Residents and visitors relax on a beach on the outskirts of Odesa as smoke from a fire rises in the background following a Russian missile strike. Russia has been accused of violating Polish airspace after a missile exploded in a field in the east of the country, triggering Nato air defences, in the midst of a massive air raid that killed 13 people in neighbouring Ukraine . Photograph: Kostiantyn Liberov/Libkos/Getty Images Share View image in fullscreen Ares, France Firefighting vehicles line up along a road to suppress a wildfire near Ares. Global heating made hot, dry and windy weather at least 20 times more likely in Spain and twice as likely in France, experts from the World Weather Attribution (WWA) consortium have calculated . The finding is the latest to pin the blame for the continent’s sweltering and deadly summer firmly on the heating caused by the burning of oil, gas and coal. Photograph: Baz Ratner/AFP/Getty Images Share View image in fullscreen Saumos, France Firefighters and civilian volunteers refill a water tanker during night-time wildfire suppression operations in Gironde. Severe wildfires have burned across Spain and France since early July, killing people, destroying thousands of homes and forcing more than 300,000 people to flee . Photograph: Fabrice Sapte /ABACA/Shutterstock Share View image in fullscreen Ceuta, Spain Migrants try to cross from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta. At least 57 people died trying to reach the Spanish enclave of Ceuta after as many as 50,000 migrants entered the tiny territory from Morocco in a matter of hours, triggering a political crisis for the Madrid government and unleashing a barrage of criticism from other EU countries. Photograph: Antonio Sempere/AP Share View image in fullscreen Fnideq, Morocco A member of the security forces stands guard as people attempt to cross from the northern Moroccan town of Fnideq to the Spanish enclave of Ceuta. Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez , who arrived in Ceuta on Friday, described the influx of as many as 50,000 migrants as ‘a violation of Spain’s territorial integrity’ and said he would use all the state resources at his disposal to guarantee the safety of the people of Ceuta. Photograph: AP Share View image in fullscreen Gaza Palestinians take cover following an Israeli airstrike in Gaza. Donald Trump has declared a breakthrough in negotiations over the disarmament of Hamas and the withdrawal of Israeli forces but Israel has yet to respond officially to the plan and government officials have voiced scepticism over the deal. Photograph: Mohammed Saber/EPA Share View image in fullscreen Deir al-Balah, Gaza Adults and children survey the wreckage of homes destroyed in an Israeli military attack in Deir al-Balah. Israel has pointed to Hamas’s failure to disarm as justification for its continued strikes and refusal to allow any reconstruction in Gaza, and for Israeli forces’ steady edging forward from the demarcation line agreed in October. Photograph: Ali Jadallah/Anadolu/Getty Images Share View image in fullscreen Qusra, West Bank Children stand outside a mosque that was burned during an attack by Israeli settlers in the West Bank village of Qusra. On its wall, Hebrew graffiti reads ‘Revenge Benayahu’, referring to an Israeli settler killed during clashes with Palestinians in the village of Tell. Photograph: Léo Corrêa/AP Share View image in fullscreen Anzah, West Bank Palestinians gather in front of a building containing shops and flats that were demolished by Israeli forces, citing the lack of a building permit, in Anzah. Israel said it was preparing a major military operation in the West Bank after four Palestinians and two Israelis were killed during a confrontation that began after armed settlers entered a Palestinian village with support from the Israeli military. Photograph: John Wessels/AFP/Getty Images Share View image in fullscreen Yatsushiro, Japan A man walks past collapsed houses in Yatsushiro following the 28 July earthquake. The death toll from the powerful quake has risen to 30 , as the search continues for survivors trapped in a badly damaged shopping centre, a paper mill and collapsed homes across the south-west of the country. Photograph: Yuichi Yamazaki/AFP/Getty Images Share View image in fullscreen Menasha, Wisconsin, US Residents survey damage after a tornado ripped through the town of Menasha. A rare and powerful tornado developed over north-east Wisconsin on Monday, lasting 26 minutes and carving a 12-mile path of destruction in western parts of Appleton and Menasha before dissipating over Lake Winnebago. Photograph: Scott Olson/Getty Images Share View image in fullscreen Central Valley of California, US Aurora and her six-year-old daughter, who were detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement and sent to a family detention centre in Texas, pose for a portrait with Aurora’s ankle monitor in the Central Valley of California. The Trump administration arrested a record number of immigrants last month , according to newly released government data that reveals how US immigration agents are quietly but steadily ramping up operations across the country. Photograph: Carlos Barría/Reuters Share View image in fullscreen Pyongyang, North Korea Youths and students dance at the plaza of the Arch of Triumph to mark the 73rd anniversary of the end of the Korean War in Pyongyang. Russia and North Korea are close to completing a bridge that will form the first road link ever built between the countries, amid concerns the two increasingly close allies are creating infrastructure to boost military cooperation in the Ukraine war. Photograph: Kim Won Jin/AFP/Getty Images Share View image in fullscreen Nairobi, Kenya Revellers in cowboy attire dance to country music during International Cowboy Day celebrations at Ngong racecourse. Observed annually on the fourth Saturday of July, International Cowboy Day celebrates the history, culture and enduring legacy of cowboys and cowgirls around the world. Photograph: Luis Tato/AFP/Getty Images Share View image in fullscreen Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, Spain US photographer Spencer Tunick gives instructions to the participants of his new performance. Entitled Gran Spectrum, it’s a tribute to the gay community, with participants painted in the colours of the rainbow flag. Photograph: Angel Medina G/EPA Share View image in fullscreen Paris, France The peloton cycles up Rue Lepic on the ascent of the Butte de Montmartre during the 21st stage of the 113th edition of the Tour de France . Tadej Pogačar took a record-equalling fifth win on Sunday, joining Jacques Anquetil, Eddy Merckx, Bernard Hinault and Miguel Induráin in the canon of the Tour’s most successful cyclists. Photograph: Geoffroy van der Hasselt/AFP/Getty Images Share View image in fullscreen Glasgow, Scotland Team Australia compete in the men’s 4000m team pursuit qualifying during the Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games at Sir Chris Hoy velodrome. Photograph: Quinn Rooney/Getty Images Share View image in fullscreen Bray, England The green square and parched, dry and yellow grass on the cricket field of Maidenhead & Bray cricket club during a game in Bray. England is on track to record its highest ever number of heat-related deaths this summer after the UK Health Security Agency announced that an estimated 2,877 people had died in the May and June heatwaves. https://www.dw.com/en/hungary-eu-commiss.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5N692 European Commission President von der Leyen says Hungary should be rewarded for reforms undertaken to address standing problems Image: Omar Havana/REUTERS Advertisement The European Commission on Wednesday proposed unlocking some €4.2 billion ($4.8 billion) in frozen funds to be paid out to Hungary . The cash had been blocked over allegations of corruption tied to Hungary's former government, led by Viktor Orban and his Fidesz party. "Hungary has taken important steps to strengthen the rule of law and protect the [European] Union's financial interests," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in a statement. A Commission press release said reforms implemented after Hungary elected Peter Magyar prime minister had addressed "shortcomings in areas such as public procurement, the anti-corruption framework, risks of conflicts of interest and the effectiveness of prosecutorial action." Orban, a feverent critic of the EU , was often at odds with the bloc over accusations that he and his cronies had undermined rule of law and democracy in the country and that he had engaged in self-dealing and corruption — all charges that he vehemently denied. The Commission said that steps taken by the new Magyar government to rectify prior problems should result in funds being partially unfrozen and the country once again being allowed to participate in European academic exchange and research programs. In May, the Commission said it was prepared to unfreeze a total of €16.4 billion in earmarked funds should Budapest make good on its promises to implement all proposed reforms. EU member states must now approve the Commission's plan.
